claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires processing temperatures above 2300 °C.
Earlier lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens without Si doping remain vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation.
Earlier lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens without Si doping remain vulnerable to liquid plating-metal corrosion.
Adding 2–4 wt% Si to ZrB2 and reactively hot pressing at approximately 1700 °C will form a borosilicate glass phase.
The resulting borosilicate glass will be uniformly distributed as a continuous grain-boundary phase.
During sintering, added Si reacts with available boron to produce the borosilicate glass.
The borosilicate phase acts as a liquid-phase sintering aid.
The liquid-phase sintering aid will enable full densification at approximately 1700 °C.
The grain-boundary glass will impede oxygen penetration.
The grain-boundary glass will impede penetration by liquid plating metal.
Si-doped ZrB2 will have greater mechanical strength than conventionally processed ZrB2 and previous lower-temperature specimens.
Si-doped ZrB2 will exhibit lower elevated-temperature oxidation weight gain than conventionally processed ZrB2 and previous lower-temperature specimens.
Si-doped ZrB2 will exhibit lower corrosion rates in liquid plating-metal environments than conventionally processed ZrB2 and previous lower-temperature specimens.
The intervention is applicable when hot pressing is conducted near 1700 °C under an inert or reducing atmosphere.
The optimal Si concentration and glass-phase uniformity remain uncertain.
Long-term stability of the protective phase under thermal cycling has not been demonstrated.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that Si and available boron form an oxygen-containing borosilicate glass, but the intervention supplies elemental Si to ZrB2 and specifies an inert or reducing atmosphere without identifying an oxygen or silica source.

The experimental design includes only pure and Si-doped ZrB2 processed at approximately 1700 °C, whereas the falsification rule requires comparison with both conventionally sintered ZrB2 at at least 2300 °C and prior lower-temperature specimens. Those required comparator groups are not included in the design.
